summary: An informational memo to focus discussion on problems of running out of top-level domain names and conflicts when many organizations want the same name. It proposes a convention for using legal names as domain names.

eli5.summary: When too many people want the same name, someone has to decide who gets it. This memo suggests using the official legal name.

questions: domain name conflicts and tld exhaustion
can legal company names be used as domain names
how to avoid domain name conflicts
what does ltd.uk mean in a domain
subtitle: A proposal to hang company and trademark names under country domains so the law, not the registry, settles who owns a name.

tldr.problem: Top-level domains were running short of desirable names, and organisations with legitimate claims to the same name were in conflict, sometimes ending in costly legal action.
tldr.mechanism: The memo proposes sub-domains under each country code that mirror legal name types, such as LTD.UK or TM.FR, named from the full legal name with spaces turned into hyphens, so uniqueness comes from the company or trade mark registration authority.
tldr.outcome: It is a discussion framework, not a standard. The RFC Editor's note says it depends on corporations moving to more cumbersome names with no incentive to do so, and may not be politically feasible.

facts.label: Proposed extra gTLDs it rejects
facts.value: FIRM, STORE, WEB, ARTS, REC, INFO, NOM

today: RFC 2352 is an Informational memo that obsoletes RFC 2240. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the memo itself says it specifies no Internet standard and only frames a discussion.

sections.title: Purpose of the Memo
sections.content:
The memo is written to focus discussion on two problems: running out of names in the top level of the domain space, and conflicts when several organisations want the same name. Its proposals are a framework, meant to let a general consensus emerge and eventually lead to standards.

The RFC Editor's note adds context. This is an independent submission. The editor observes that it appears to depend on corporations changing to more cumbersome names, for example cisco-systems.co.ca.us, without an incentive such as deprecating .com and .net. It also appears to legislate how each national registry structures its space, which the document itself says is a national matter. The note concludes that it may not be politically feasible.
sections.eli5: The author is starting a conversation about who should get a name when many want it. The memo's editor warns that the idea might be hard to carry out.

sections.title: The Domain Space and Why Names Run Out
sections.content:
The domain space is a hierarchical tree with several top level domains (TLDs). They split into generic TLDs (gTLDs) and two-letter ISO 3166 country domains. How sub-domains are handed out under a TLD is entirely up to that TLD's registry, which may add structure or allocate names in a flat way.

The memo contrasts three cases. Under a flat gTLD such as COM, an organisation is clearly commercial but the country is unknown. Under a flat country domain such as FR, the country is known but not the type of organisation. Under a hierarchical country domain such as UK, sub-domains like AC and CO reveal both.

That flexibility can lead to exhaustion of names in the generic space and to conflicts between organisations that both have a legitimate claim to a name.
sections.eli5: Some name lists are one big pile and some are sorted into folders. The one big pile fills up fast, and then people fight over the good names.

sections.title: Why More gTLDs Do Not Help
sections.content:
One earlier proposal is to create more gTLDs so organisations with the same name can register under different ones: FIRM, STORE, WEB, ARTS, REC, INFO and NOM. The memo lists three disadvantages.

  • Users cannot tell which TLD belongs to which organisation. MCDONALDS.COM could be the restaurant and MCDONALDS.FIRM a law firm.
  • Big corporations would simply reserve every variation, such as IBM.COM, IBM.FIRM and IBM.STORE, making exhaustion and conflict worse.
  • Legally held names can still be acquired by anybody, so conflicts remain.

The memo also notes that the World Intellectual Property Organisation's work covers only dispute resolution for trademarks under gTLDs, not the full legal context of where a name was registered.
sections.eli5: Adding more name lists does not stop people from grabbing the same name in all of them. Big companies would just grab every copy.

sections.title: Legal-Name Sub-Domains
sections.content:
The proposal creates a functional hierarchy beneath each country TLD, built from existing identifiers for company names and trade marks in a locality, state, province or country. The general form is <legal-token>.<locality-identifier(s)>.<iso3166-country>. Examples from the memo are LTD.UK and PLC.UK for limited and public limited companies, TM.FR for trademarks in France, GMBH.DE for German companies, and, for the US, INC, LTD, CO and CORP under a state (each equivalent) plus LLC.

The registry should create entries based on that place's laws for allocating legal names. It should use the full legal name but omit the legal token, since the choice of upper-level domain supplies it. All spaces become hyphens, and other punctuation is dropped or also becomes a hyphen. Holders of international trademarks and names may use the gTLD INT in place of a country, as in TM.INT and REG.INT.

The proposal does not abolish gTLDs. A legal name should be sought first and a generic name may be used alongside it. Disputes over which organisation owns a name become a matter for the company-name or trade-mark registration authority, not the domain registry.
sections.eli5: Each country gets folders named after kinds of companies. Your folder name is your official company name, with dashes instead of spaces, so nobody else can have it.

sections.title: Other Sub-Domains, Scripts and Logos
sections.content:
In countries without existing sub-structure, the memo strongly recommends also creating sub-domains for commercial entities, organisations and academic entities (for example AC/EDU, CO/COM and OR/ORG), to reduce conflicts from organisations that are not legally registered.

Names stay limited to the ASCII letters, digits and hyphen described in RFC 1035, so names in other scripts are bound by that definition or any future update. Non-textual trade marks such as logos or three dimensional shapes are beyond the scope of the memo, though their use is not explicitly prohibited.
sections.eli5: Groups that are not registered companies still get folders of their own. Names can only use basic letters, numbers and dashes, and logos are left out.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo says it raises no issues relating to network security. It adds one requirement: when delegating entries in these sub-domains, registries must make sure an application contains sufficient evidence of the legal rights to the name being requested.
sections.eli5: Before giving out a name, the registry must check that the person asking really has the legal right to it.
